title: Environment
description: Vocabulario para essays y debates sobre cambio climático, contaminación y sostenibilidad.

cards.definition: The amount of carbon dioxide released by a person's or organisation's activities.
cards.example: Individuals can reduce their carbon footprint by flying less and eating less meat.

cards.definition: Gases released into the air, especially by vehicles and factories.
cards.example: Transport accounts for nearly a quarter of global greenhouse gas emissions.

cards.definition: Fuels such as coal, oil and gas formed from ancient organisms.
cards.example: Our continued dependence on fossil fuels is the main driver of climate change.

cards.definition: Energy from sources that are naturally replaced, like wind and sun.
cards.example: Governments should subsidise renewable energy to make it competitive with coal.

cards.definition: Able to continue without damaging the environment or using up resources.
cards.example: Cities must adopt more sustainable forms of transport.

cards.definition: The cutting down of forests on a large scale.
cards.example: Deforestation in the Amazon threatens thousands of species.

cards.definition: The variety of plant and animal life in an area.
cards.example: Intensive farming has led to a sharp loss of biodiversity.

cards.definition: Animals or plants at risk of disappearing.
cards.example: Zoos can play a role in breeding endangered species.

cards.definition: The natural home of an animal or plant.
cards.example: Urban expansion has destroyed the natural habitats of many birds.

cards.definition: Harmful substances in air, water or soil / a substance that pollutes.
cards.example: Air pollution in large cities causes serious respiratory illnesses.

cards.definition: The gradual increase in the Earth's average temperature.
cards.example: Global warming is causing glaciers to melt at an alarming rate.

cards.definition: Unusually severe weather such as floods, droughts and heatwaves.
cards.example: Extreme weather events are becoming more frequent and more intense.

cards.definition: A long period without rain.
cards.example: Prolonged droughts have devastated crops across southern Europe.

cards.definition: To process used materials so they can be used again.
cards.example: Recycling alone cannot solve the problem; we must also consume less.

cards.definition: Plastic items used once and thrown away.
cards.example: Several countries have banned single-use plastics such as straws and bags.

cards.definition: A place where waste is buried in the ground.
cards.example: Millions of tonnes of food end up in landfill every year.

cards.definition: The protection of the natural environment.
cards.example: Ecotourism can generate funds for wildlife conservation.

cards.definition: To reduce something until little is left.
cards.example: Overfishing has severely depleted fish stocks in the North Atlantic.

cards.definition: To make something bad less severe.
cards.example: Planting trees can help mitigate the effects of urban heat.

cards.definition: Not harmful to the environment.
cards.es: ecológico, respetuoso con el medio ambiente
cards.example: Consumers are willing to pay more for eco-friendly products.

cards.definition: A tax on fuels according to the carbon they emit.
cards.example: A carbon tax would encourage companies to invest in cleaner technology.

cards.definition: Impossible to change back.
cards.example: Scientists warn that some damage to coral reefs may be irreversible.

cards.definition: All the living things in an area and how they interact.
cards.example: Introducing foreign species can disrupt fragile ecosystems.

cards.definition: Aware of and concerned about the environment.
cards.example: Younger generations tend to be more environmentally conscious than their parents.

title: Education
description: Vocabulario sobre colegios, universidad, métodos de enseñanza y acceso a la educación.

cards.definition: The subjects included in a course of study.
cards.example: Financial literacy should be part of the school curriculum.

cards.definition: Required by law or rules.
cards.example: Physical education should remain compulsory until the age of sixteen.

cards.definition: Education at university or college level.
cards.example: Access to higher education has expanded dramatically in recent decades.

cards.definition: Money paid for being taught at a university or school.
cards.example: High tuition fees may discourage students from poorer backgrounds.

cards.definition: Learning by repetition and memorisation rather than understanding.
cards.example: Critics argue that rote learning does not prepare students for real-world problems.

cards.definition: The ability to analyse information and form judgements.
cards.example: Schools should place greater emphasis on critical thinking than on memorisation.

cards.definition: How well a student does in their studies.
cards.example: Research links regular sleep to better academic performance.

cards.definition: Education that prepares people for a specific trade or job.
cards.example: Vocational training offers a valuable alternative to university.

cards.definition: Studying remotely, usually over the internet.
cards.example: Online learning gives working adults the flexibility to gain new qualifications.

cards.definition: The ability to read and write / to work with numbers.
cards.example: Early literacy programmes have a lasting impact on children's development.

cards.definition: The number of students in a class.
cards.example: Reducing class sizes allows teachers to give more individual attention.

cards.definition: Activities outside normal lessons, such as sports and clubs.
cards.example: Extracurricular activities help pupils develop teamwork and confidence.

cards.definition: Having a wide range of skills and experience.
cards.example: Arts subjects help produce well-rounded individuals.

cards.definition: Tests given and marked in the same way for all students.
cards.example: An overemphasis on standardised testing encourages teachers to 'teach to the test'.

cards.definition: To leave school or university before finishing.
cards.example: Financial pressure forces many students to drop out of university.

cards.definition: Continuing to learn throughout one's life.
cards.example: In a rapidly changing economy, lifelong learning is essential.

cards.definition: Classes with students of different levels together.
cards.es: clases con alumnos de distintos niveles
cards.example: Some argue that mixed-ability classes hold back the most gifted students.

cards.definition: Having exceptional natural ability.
cards.example: Gifted children may become bored if lessons are not challenging enough.

cards.definition: Money given to a student to pay for their studies.
cards.example: Scholarships allow talented students from low-income families to attend university.

cards.definition: A person with a university degree; to complete a degree.
cards.example: Many graduates struggle to find jobs related to their degree.
cards.warning: 'graduate FROM university', no 'graduate university' (salvo uso US informal).

cards.definition: Exams passed or courses completed.
cards.example: Employers increasingly value practical skills over formal qualifications.

cards.definition: Training people to obey rules; controlled behaviour.
cards.example: Teachers today struggle to maintain discipline in large classes.

cards.definition: Influence from people of the same age to behave like them.
cards.example: Peer pressure can lead teenagers to neglect their studies.

cards.definition: Involving active participation and practical experience.
cards.example: Hands-on experiments make science more engaging for young learners.

title: Technology
description: Inteligencia artificial, internet, redes sociales y su impacto en la sociedad.

cards.definition: Computer systems able to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence.
cards.example: Artificial intelligence is likely to transform sectors such as healthcare and law.

cards.definition: The use of machines to do work previously done by people.
cards.example: Automation threatens many routine jobs in manufacturing.

cards.definition: The most advanced.
cards.example: The university has invested in cutting-edge research facilities.

cards.definition: The gap between people who have access to technology and those who do not.
cards.example: The pandemic exposed the digital divide between rich and poor students.

cards.definition: The right to keep personal information private.
cards.example: Tech companies collect vast amounts of personal data, raising serious privacy concerns.

cards.definition: Close watching of people, often by governments or companies.
cards.example: Facial recognition has made mass surveillance easier than ever.

cards.definition: Time spent using devices / compulsive use of technology.
cards.es: tiempo frente a pantallas / adicción a la tecnología
cards.example: Excessive screen time has been linked to poor sleep in teenagers.

cards.definition: Websites and apps for sharing content and networking.
cards.example: Social media platforms have been criticised for spreading misinformation.
cards.warning: 'social media' es incontable o plural: 'social media is/are', no 'a social media'.

cards.definition: False or misleading information.
cards.example: Misinformation spreads faster online than accurate reporting.

cards.definition: Crime committed using computers or the internet.
cards.example: Cybercrime costs businesses billions of dollars each year.

cards.definition: A new idea, method or invention.
cards.example: Government funding can encourage technological innovation.

cards.definition: No longer used because something newer exists.
cards.example: Many skills taught today may become obsolete within a decade.

cards.definition: Easy to use or understand.
cards.example: Banking apps have become more user-friendly, encouraging older people to use them.

cards.definition: Knowing a lot about modern technology.
cards.es: experto en tecnología, ducho en tecnología
cards.example: Today's children are far more tech-savvy than their grandparents.

cards.definition: Working from home or another place away from the office.
cards.example: Remote working reduces commuting but can blur the line between work and home.

cards.definition: An important discovery or development.
cards.example: Recent breakthroughs in battery technology could make electric cars cheaper.

cards.definition: A set of rules a computer follows to solve a problem or make decisions.
cards.example: Algorithms decide which posts users see, which can create echo chambers.

cards.definition: An environment where people only hear opinions that match their own.
cards.example: Online echo chambers may contribute to political polarisation.

cards.definition: Electronic devices worn on the body, such as smartwatches.
cards.example: Wearable technology allows people to monitor their health in real time.

cards.definition: Depending too much on something.
cards.example: Over-reliance on calculators may weaken children's basic maths skills.

cards.definition: To make a process simpler and more efficient.
cards.example: Digital systems have streamlined many administrative tasks.

cards.definition: The ability to connect to the internet or other systems.
cards.example: Poor connectivity in rural areas holds back local businesses.

cards.definition: Communication in person rather than through technology.
cards.example: Some fear that social media is replacing meaningful face-to-face interaction.

cards.definition: Something with both advantages and disadvantages.
cards.example: Technology is a double-edged sword: it connects us but also isolates us.
cards.note: Una de las pocas expresiones idiomáticas que funcionan bien en Task 2, sin abusar.

title: Health
description: Estilo de vida, sanidad pública, enfermedades y prevención.

cards.definition: A way of life involving little physical activity.
cards.example: Sedentary lifestyles are a major cause of obesity among office workers.

cards.definition: The condition of being very overweight.
cards.example: Childhood obesity has tripled in many countries since the 1980s.

cards.definition: A diet containing the right amounts of different foods.
cards.example: A balanced diet can prevent many chronic diseases.

cards.definition: A long-lasting medical condition.
cards.example: Chronic diseases such as diabetes place a huge burden on health systems.

cards.definition: The average number of years a person is expected to live.
cards.example: Life expectancy has risen thanks to better sanitation and medicine.

cards.definition: Healthcare that aims to stop diseases before they start.
cards.example: Investing in prevention is cheaper than treating illnesses later.

cards.definition: Healthcare provided by the state and funded by taxes.
cards.example: A strong public healthcare system ensures that treatment does not depend on income.

cards.definition: A person's psychological and emotional condition.
cards.example: Employers are increasingly aware of the importance of staff wellbeing.

cards.definition: Caused by stress.
cards.example: Stress-related illnesses are a leading cause of absence from work.

cards.definition: Giving people a vaccine to protect them from a disease.
cards.example: Mass vaccination programmes have eradicated smallpox.

cards.definition: A disease affecting many people in one area / worldwide.
cards.example: The pandemic revealed weaknesses in many countries' health systems.

cards.definition: Food changed industrially, often high in sugar, salt and fat.
cards.example: Taxing junk food could encourage healthier eating habits.

cards.definition: A tax on drinks or foods with high sugar content.
cards.example: Since the sugar tax was introduced, sales of fizzy drinks have fallen.

cards.definition: Being healthy and strong through exercise.
cards.example: Schools should promote physical fitness through daily sports.

cards.definition: A population with an increasing proportion of older people.
cards.example: An ageing population will put pressure on healthcare budgets.

cards.definition: Lists of patients waiting for treatment.
cards.example: Long waiting lists push some patients towards private healthcare.

cards.definition: Unwanted effects of a medicine or treatment.
cards.example: All medicines carry a risk of side effects.

cards.definition: Treatments outside conventional medicine.
cards.example: There is little scientific evidence that alternative medicine is effective.

cards.definition: Able to cause death.
cards.example: Air pollution can trigger life-threatening asthma attacks.

cards.definition: A heavy load or responsibility for.
cards.example: Smoking-related diseases are a huge burden on the health service.

cards.definition: The balance between time spent working and personal life.
cards.es: conciliación de la vida laboral y personal
cards.example: A healthy work-life balance reduces burnout.

cards.definition: Exhaustion caused by long-term stress, usually at work.
cards.example: Doctors and nurses are at high risk of burnout.

cards.definition: Public campaign to inform people about health risks.
cards.example: Health awareness campaigns have helped reduce smoking rates.

cards.definition: Causing harm or damage.
cards.example: Lack of sleep is detrimental to both physical and mental health.

title: Work & employment
description: Empleo, desempleo, condiciones laborales y el futuro del trabajo.

cards.definition: The state of not having a job; the number of people without jobs.
cards.example: Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high in southern Europe.

cards.definition: Confidence that you will not lose your job.
cards.example: Many young workers value job security more than a high salary.

cards.definition: The feeling of enjoyment and fulfilment from your work.
cards.example: Job satisfaction depends on recognition as much as on pay.

cards.definition: A labour market of short-term, freelance or app-based jobs.
cards.es: economía de plataformas, trabajo por encargo
cards.example: Workers in the gig economy often lack sick pay and pensions.
collocations: the rise of the gig economy

cards.definition: Working for yourself rather than for one employer.
cards.example: Freelance work offers flexibility but an unstable income.

cards.definition: The lowest pay allowed by law.
cards.example: Raising the minimum wage could reduce in-work poverty.

cards.definition: All the people working in a country, industry or company.
cards.example: Women now make up almost half of the workforce.

cards.definition: Work requiring / not requiring special training.
cards.es: mano de obra cualificada / no cualificada
cards.example: Automation is reducing demand for unskilled labour.

cards.definition: Chances of success and promotion in a career.
cards.example: A second language can significantly improve your career prospects.

cards.definition: A move to a higher position at work.
cards.example: Women are still less likely than men to receive a promotion.

cards.definition: Arrangements allowing employees to choose when they work.
cards.example: Flexible working hours help parents balance work and childcare.

cards.definition: The amount of work produced in a period of time.
cards.example: Some trials suggest that a four-day week does not reduce productivity.

cards.definition: To lose your job because the employer no longer needs you.
cards.example: Thousands of factory workers were laid off when the plant closed.
cards.note: 'made redundant' es británico; 'laid off' más americano.

cards.definition: To learn new skills for a different or better job.
cards.example: Governments should help workers retrain as traditional industries decline.

cards.definition: Not enough workers to fill available jobs.
cards.example: Many rich countries face labour shortages in nursing and construction.

cards.definition: To travel regularly between home and work; that journey.
cards.example: Long commutes reduce the time people can spend with their families.

cards.definition: Extra advantages given with a job, besides salary.
cards.example: Tech companies attract staff with perks such as free meals and gym membership.

cards.definition: An invisible barrier preventing women or minorities from reaching top jobs.
cards.example: Despite progress, many women still hit a glass ceiling in corporate careers.

cards.definition: The difference between the average earnings of men and women.
cards.example: Publishing salary data could help close the gender pay gap.

cards.definition: A person who starts a business / the activity of doing so.
cards.example: Low taxes and simple regulations encourage entrepreneurship.

cards.definition: The amount of work a person has to do.
cards.example: Heavy workloads are driving many teachers out of the profession.

cards.definition: Giving satisfaction and a sense of purpose.
cards.example: Many people would accept lower pay for a more fulfilling job.

cards.definition: Keeping employees from leaving.
cards.example: Training opportunities improve staff retention.

cards.definition: Office / manual jobs.
cards.example: AI may affect white-collar jobs as much as blue-collar ones.

title: Globalisation & economy
description: Comercio, crecimiento, desigualdad y empresas multinacionales.

cards.definition: The increasing connection of economies and cultures worldwide.
cards.example: Globalisation has lifted millions out of poverty but also increased inequality within countries.

cards.definition: A company operating in many countries.
cards.example: Multinational corporations often move production to countries with lower wages.

cards.definition: An increase in the production of goods and services.
cards.example: Rapid economic growth often comes at an environmental cost.

cards.definition: Trade between countries without tariffs or restrictions.
cards.example: Supporters of free trade argue that it lowers prices for consumers.

cards.definition: A tax on imported goods.
cards.example: Raising tariffs can protect local industries but provoke trade wars.

cards.definition: Unequal distribution of income in a population.
cards.example: Income inequality has widened in most developed countries since the 1980s.

cards.definition: Poorer, industrialising / richer, industrialised nations.
cards.es: países en vías de desarrollo / desarrollados
cards.example: Developed countries should help developing countries adapt to climate change.
cards.warning: Evita 'third-world countries': suena anticuado y peyorativo.

cards.definition: To pay an outside company, often abroad, to do work.
cards.example: Many firms outsource customer service to reduce costs.

cards.definition: A period of economic decline.
cards.example: During a recession, young people are often the first to lose their jobs.

cards.definition: The general rise in prices / the money needed for basic expenses.
cards.example: Rising inflation has caused a cost-of-living crisis for many families.

cards.definition: A culture focused on buying goods.
cards.example: Consumerism encourages people to replace products that still work.

cards.definition: The amount of goods money can buy.
cards.example: Stagnant wages have reduced the purchasing power of the middle class.

cards.definition: The minimum income needed to meet basic needs.
cards.example: Millions of people still live below the poverty line.

cards.definition: The process by which local cultures become more alike.
cards.example: Critics blame globalisation for the cultural homogenisation of city centres.

cards.definition: Depending on each other.
cards.example: In an interdependent world, a crisis in one country quickly spreads.

cards.definition: The network of producers and transport that delivers a product.
cards.example: The pandemic revealed how fragile global supply chains are.

cards.definition: Money invested in a country by foreign companies or people.
cards.example: Low corporate taxes attract foreign investment.

cards.definition: To treat workers unfairly for profit.
cards.example: Some clothing brands have been accused of exploiting workers in poorer countries.

cards.definition: The emigration of highly skilled people.
cards.example: Low salaries for researchers have caused a brain drain from southern Europe.

cards.definition: Public funds raised through taxation.
cards.example: Spending taxpayers' money on a new stadium is hard to justify.

cards.definition: The level of wealth and comfort people have.
cards.example: Industrialisation raised the standard of living for most citizens.

cards.definition: To help the economy grow.
cards.example: Hosting the Olympics is often claimed to boost the local economy.

cards.definition: Small companies serving a local area.
cards.example: Large supermarkets can drive local businesses out of the market.

cards.definition: Trade that pays producers in poorer countries a fair price.
cards.example: Fair trade products guarantee farmers a minimum price for their crops.

cards.definition: A person who has committed a crime.
cards.example: Young offenders should be given education rather than long prison sentences.

cards.definition: To commit a crime again.
cards.example: Prisoners who learn a trade are less likely to reoffend.

cards.definition: Helping criminals return to normal life in society.
cards.example: Prisons should focus on rehabilitation, not just punishment.

cards.definition: Something that discourages people from doing something.
cards.example: There is little evidence that harsh sentences act as a deterrent.

cards.definition: A punishment given by a court; to give such a punishment.
cards.example: He was sentenced to five years in prison for fraud.

cards.definition: Unpaid work in the community given as a punishment.
cards.example: Community service may be more effective than prison for minor crimes.

cards.definition: Minor crime, such as shoplifting.
cards.example: Petty crime tends to rise in areas with high unemployment.

cards.definition: Crime involving physical force against people.
cards.example: Violent crime has fallen in most Western cities over the last thirty years.

cards.definition: The number of crimes in a period relative to population.
cards.example: Better street lighting has helped lower the crime rate.

cards.definition: Crime committed by young people.
cards.example: Youth clubs can help prevent juvenile delinquency.

cards.definition: The police and agencies that make people obey the law.
cards.example: Law enforcement agencies need more resources to tackle cybercrime.

cards.definition: Execution as a legal punishment.
cards.example: Opponents of capital punishment point out the risk of executing innocent people.

cards.definition: The fundamental reasons behind a problem.
cards.example: To reduce crime, we must address its root causes, such as poverty and lack of education.

cards.definition: Favouring strict punishments.
cards.example: Politicians often promise to be tough on crime to win votes.

cards.definition: Too many inmates for the space available.
cards.example: Prison overcrowding makes rehabilitation almost impossible.

cards.definition: A person kept in prison.
cards.example: Inmates who receive education have better job prospects on release.

cards.definition: A person harmed by a crime.
cards.example: The justice system should give more support to victims of crime.

cards.definition: Closed-circuit television cameras used for security.
cards.example: CCTV in public places may deter crime but raises privacy concerns.

cards.definition: To do something illegal.
cards.example: People who commit minor offences should not mix with serious criminals.

cards.definition: The courts, laws and institutions that deliver justice.
cards.example: Public trust in the justice system depends on fair and fast trials.

cards.definition: A legal process to decide guilt / the place where it happens.
cards.example: Every defendant has the right to a fair trial.

cards.definition: Officially judged to have / not have committed a crime.
cards.example: Anyone found guilty of drink-driving should lose their licence.

cards.definition: Money paid as a punishment; to make someone pay this.
cards.example: Companies that pollute rivers should face heavy fines.

cards.definition: Behaviour that disturbs or harms others, like vandalism.
cards.example: Boredom among teenagers is often linked to anti-social behaviour.

title: Cities & housing
description: Urbanismo, vivienda, servicios urbanos y vida en la ciudad frente al campo.

cards.definition: The movement of people from rural areas to cities.
cards.example: Rapid urbanisation has put pressure on housing and transport.

cards.definition: The uncontrolled spread of a city into surrounding countryside.
cards.example: Urban sprawl increases car dependency and destroys farmland.

cards.definition: Homes that people on average or low incomes can afford.
cards.example: The lack of affordable housing forces young people to live with their parents.

cards.definition: Not enough homes for the population.
cards.example: A severe housing shortage has pushed rents to record levels.

cards.definition: The cost of buying homes / rapidly rising rents.
cards.es: precio de la vivienda / alquileres disparados
cards.example: Soaring rents in the city centre have driven families to the suburbs.

cards.definition: Wealthier people moving into a poorer area, changing it and raising prices.
cards.example: Gentrification has improved some neighbourhoods but pushed out long-term residents.

cards.definition: Basic systems such as roads, water and power supplies.
cards.example: Many cities' infrastructure was not designed for their current populations.

cards.definition: Useful or pleasant services such as parks, shops and libraries.
cards.example: New housing estates often lack basic amenities like schools and clinics.

cards.definition: Areas of grass, trees and plants in a city.
cards.example: Access to green spaces improves residents' mental health.

cards.definition: Too many vehicles causing slow traffic.
cards.example: Traffic congestion costs the economy billions in lost working hours.

cards.definition: With too many people / many people per area.
cards.example: Densely populated cities can provide public transport more efficiently.

cards.definition: Residential areas on the edge of a city.
cards.example: Many families move to the suburbs in search of bigger homes.

cards.definition: The state of having no home.
cards.example: Rising rents have led to a sharp increase in homelessness.

cards.definition: Improving run-down parts of a city.
cards.example: Urban regeneration projects transformed the old docks into a cultural district.

cards.definition: In poor condition / lacking money and services.
cards.example: Investment should target the most deprived neighbourhoods.

cards.definition: Tall buildings with many floors.
cards.example: High-rise buildings allow more people to live in less space.

cards.definition: An area where cars are not allowed.
cards.example: Pedestrianised zones make city centres safer and more pleasant.

cards.definition: The design and organisation of cities.
cards.example: Good urban planning can reduce the need to drive.

cards.definition: How good and comfortable people's lives are.
cards.example: Smaller towns often offer a higher quality of life than big cities.

cards.definition: The decline in population of rural areas.
cards.example: Remote work could help reverse rural depopulation.

cards.definition: Harmful or annoying levels of noise.
cards.example: Noise pollution from traffic disturbs sleep for millions of city dwellers.

cards.definition: People who live in cities.
cards.example: City dwellers have easier access to cultural events.

cards.definition: Full of life and energy / full of busy activity.
cards.example: The old town has a vibrant nightlife and bustling markets.
cards.note: Muy útil en Speaking Part 2 para describir lugares.

cards.definition: Buildings or areas combining homes, shops and offices.
cards.example: Mixed-use developments reduce commuting by placing jobs near homes.

title: Transport
description: Transporte público, coches, aviación y movilidad sostenible.

cards.definition: Buses, trains and trams available to everyone.
cards.example: Investing in public transport is the most effective way to reduce congestion.

cards.definition: A person who travels regularly to work.
cards.es: persona que se desplaza a diario al trabajo
cards.example: Commuters waste hours each week stuck in traffic.

cards.definition: The busiest times of day for traffic.
cards.example: Trains are overcrowded during rush hour.

cards.definition: Having one's own car.
cards.example: Car ownership among young urban adults has fallen.

cards.definition: Designed so that people need a car for most journeys.
cards.example: Many American suburbs are entirely car-dependent.

cards.definition: A fee for driving into a busy city centre.
cards.example: London's congestion charge significantly reduced traffic in the centre.

cards.definition: Parts of the road reserved for bicycles.
cards.example: Safe cycle lanes encourage more people to cycle to work.

cards.definition: Vehicles powered by batteries rather than fuel.
cards.example: Electric vehicles produce no exhaust fumes, but their batteries require rare minerals.

cards.definition: Gases released by vehicle engines.
cards.example: Exhaust fumes are a major cause of poor air quality in cities.

cards.definition: To pay part of the cost to reduce the price.
cards.example: Governments should subsidise rail fares to make trains cheaper than flying.

cards.definition: The price of a journey on public transport.
cards.example: Free fares for students could reduce car use.

cards.definition: Fast trains, usually over 250 km/h.
cards.example: High-speed rail is a greener alternative to short-haul flights.

cards.definition: Short / long-distance flights.
cards.example: France has banned some short-haul flights where a train alternative exists.

cards.definition: Preventing accidents on roads.
cards.example: Lower speed limits have improved road safety near schools.

cards.definition: The maximum legal speed on a road.
cards.example: Many cities have introduced a 30 km/h speed limit.

cards.definition: Sharing car journeys or cars among several people.
cards.example: Car-sharing schemes reduce the number of vehicles on the road.

cards.definition: Connections by road, rail, etc. between places.
cards.example: Good transport links attract businesses to a region.

cards.definition: Traffic so heavy that it cannot move.
cards.example: Without investment in rail, the city will face constant gridlock.

cards.definition: The ability to move or travel freely.
cards.example: Accessible buses improve mobility for elderly and disabled people.

cards.definition: Vehicles that drive without a human driver.
cards.example: Self-driving cars could reduce accidents caused by human error.

cards.definition: Able to be trusted / on time.
cards.example: People will only leave their cars if trains are reliable and punctual.

cards.definition: Producing a lot of carbon dioxide.
cards.example: Aviation is one of the most carbon-intensive forms of travel.

cards.definition: A system of car parks outside a city with buses to the centre.
cards.example: Park-and-ride schemes keep cars out of historic centres.

cards.definition: Easy to reach or use, including for disabled people.
cards.example: All new stations must be accessible to wheelchair users.

title: Culture & arts
description: Arte, museos, patrimonio, tradiciones y financiación cultural.

cards.definition: Traditions, buildings and objects passed down through generations.
cards.example: Governments have a duty to protect their country's cultural heritage.

cards.definition: Long-established beliefs and practices.
cards.example: Globalisation threatens many local traditions and customs.

cards.definition: Money given to support the arts.
cards.example: Cuts to arts funding have forced several theatres to close.

cards.definition: Partly paid for by the government.
cards.example: State-subsidised museums can offer free entry to everyone.

cards.definition: A public display of art or objects.
cards.example: The museum's new exhibition attracted over 200,000 visitors.

cards.definition: Art forms performed live, such as theatre, dance and music.
cards.example: Schools should give pupils more opportunities to try the performing arts.

cards.definition: Painting, sculpture and similar arts.
cards.example: Studying the visual arts develops creativity and observation.

cards.definition: The ability to produce new ideas / expressing one's feelings.
cards.example: Art lessons give children a valuable outlet for self-expression.

cards.definition: A sense of belonging to a particular culture.
cards.example: Language is central to a community's cultural identity.

cards.definition: The existence of many different cultures.
cards.example: Cultural diversity enriches city life through food, music and festivals.

cards.definition: Including people of many cultures.
cards.example: London is one of the most multicultural cities in the world.

cards.definition: Accepted by or popular with most people.
cards.example: Streaming services tend to promote mainstream music over local artists.

cards.definition: An outstanding work of art.
cards.example: Millions of tourists queue to see the masterpieces in the Prado.

cards.definition: Objects made by people, especially of historical interest.
cards.example: Some argue that museums should return artefacts taken during colonial times.

cards.definition: Not physical but still valuable.
cards.example: The benefits of the arts are often intangible and difficult to measure.

cards.definition: To keep something in its original state.
cards.example: Historic buildings should be preserved for future generations.

cards.definition: Art painted in public places.
cards.example: Whether graffiti is art or vandalism remains a matter of debate.

cards.definition: Intellectual / popular and unsophisticated (culture).
cards.example: Opera is often seen as highbrow entertainment for the elite.

cards.definition: The ability of everyone to enjoy cultural activities.
cards.example: Free museum entry widens access to the arts for low-income families.

cards.definition: Skill in making things by hand / items made by hand.
cards.example: Tourism can help keep traditional handicrafts alive.

cards.definition: An organised celebration of art, music or traditions.
cards.example: Cultural festivals boost local economies and community pride.

cards.definition: Making people think seriously.
cards.example: The documentary was thought-provoking and changed my view on fast fashion.
cards.note: Muy útil en Speaking Part 2 (películas, libros, exposiciones).

cards.definition: Something left by people from the past.
cards.example: The Roman legacy is still visible in the town's architecture.

cards.definition: Controlling or banning content considered unacceptable.
cards.example: Artistic freedom suffers under strict censorship.

title: Government & society
description: Políticas públicas, impuestos, servicios sociales y responsabilidad ciudadana.

cards.definition: Laws, or the process of making laws.
cards.example: New legislation is needed to regulate the use of personal data.

cards.definition: To control by rules / an official rule.
cards.example: Governments should regulate the advertising of unhealthy food.

cards.definition: Money spent by the government.
cards.example: Public spending on healthcare has risen as the population ages.

cards.definition: To give money or resources for a specific purpose.
cards.example: A larger share of the budget should be allocated to education.

cards.definition: The system of taxes.
cards.example: Progressive taxation can reduce inequality.

cards.definition: A system providing state support for those in need.
cards.example: The welfare state protects citizens from extreme poverty.

cards.definition: Obligations citizens have towards society.
cards.example: Voting is widely regarded as a civic duty.

cards.definition: Members of a country / ordinary people.
cards.example: The government must consult citizens before making major changes.

cards.definition: A plan of action by a government / those who design it.
cards.example: Policymakers must balance economic growth with environmental protection.
cards.warning: 'policy' = medida concreta; 'politics' = la actividad política en general.

cards.definition: To put a plan or law into action.
cards.example: The new recycling policy was implemented in 2022.

cards.definition: To become involved to change a situation.
cards.example: Some argue that the state should not intervene in people's personal choices.

cards.definition: To officially forbid / to limit.
cards.example: Several cities have banned diesel cars from their centres.

cards.definition: Something that encourages a person to do something.
cards.example: Tax incentives could persuade companies to hire young people.

cards.definition: Required to explain actions / being responsible.
cards.es: responsable (que rinde cuentas) / rendición de cuentas
cards.example: Politicians must be held accountable for how they spend public money.

cards.definition: Dishonest behaviour by people in power.
cards.example: Corruption undermines public trust in democratic institutions.

cards.definition: Government by elected representatives.
cards.example: A free press is essential in a healthy democracy.

cards.definition: The bonds that bring a society together.
cards.example: Community centres can strengthen social cohesion in diverse neighbourhoods.

cards.definition: People excluded or at risk.
cards.example: Public policy should protect the most vulnerable groups in society.

cards.definition: Moving to live in another country / people who do so.
cards.example: Immigration can help fill labour shortages in ageing societies.

cards.definition: Becoming part of a society.
cards.example: Language classes are key to the integration of newcomers.

cards.definition: Services provided by the state, such as health and education.
cards.example: Higher taxes are justified if they fund better public services.

cards.definition: To sell a state-owned service to private companies.
cards.example: Critics argue that privatising the railways led to higher fares.

cards.definition: A government seen as too controlling of personal choices.
cards.example: Opponents call the sugar tax an example of the nanny state.

cards.definition: Involving ordinary people at a local level.
cards.example: Grassroots campaigns have pushed many councils to create cycle lanes.

title: Science & research
description: Investigación, experimentos, ética científica y exploración espacial.

cards.definition: An idea proposed as a possible explanation, to be tested.
cards.example: The researchers designed an experiment to test their hypothesis.

cards.definition: Evidence based on observation or experiment.
cards.example: There is little empirical evidence to support this claim.

cards.definition: The results of research.
cards.example: The findings suggest a strong link between diet and memory.

cards.definition: To carry out a scientific study.
cards.example: Universities conduct research that private companies would not fund.

cards.definition: Money provided for scientific research.
cards.example: Cuts in research funding threaten long-term innovation.

cards.definition: Research for knowledge itself / for practical uses.
cards.example: Pure research often leads to unexpected practical applications.

cards.definition: Evaluation of research by other experts before publication.
cards.example: Peer review helps ensure that published studies are reliable.

cards.definition: Using animals in scientific experiments.
cards.example: Animal testing remains controversial despite its role in medical progress.

cards.definition: Moral worries / a difficult moral choice.
cards.example: Genetic engineering raises serious ethical concerns.

cards.definition: Changing the genes of living things.
cards.example: Genetic modification could make crops more resistant to drought.

cards.definition: The investigation of outer space.
cards.example: Critics argue that money spent on space exploration should be used to solve problems on Earth.

cards.definition: To discover a treatment that heals a disease.
cards.example: Scientists are still trying to find a cure for Alzheimer's disease.

cards.definition: Very new and important.
cards.example: Her groundbreaking work on vaccines saved millions of lives.

cards.definition: Facts and figures / to examine them in detail.
cards.example: Researchers analysed data from over 10,000 patients.
cards.note: 'data' puede ir en plural ('data are') en estilo académico.

cards.definition: A group selected for a study / its number.
cards.example: The small sample size limits how far the results can be generalised.

cards.definition: A connection between two things / one thing causing another.
cards.example: A correlation between screen time and anxiety does not prove causation.

cards.definition: General agreement among scientists.
cards.example: There is a clear scientific consensus that human activity causes climate change.

cards.definition: Science, technology, engineering and mathematics.
cards.example: Governments are trying to attract more girls into STEM subjects.

cards.definition: A place for experiments / tests of new treatments on people.
cards.example: The drug passed three phases of clinical trials before approval.

cards.definition: Results that were not expected.
cards.example: New technologies can have unforeseen consequences for the environment.

cards.definition: Basic understanding of scientific ideas and methods.
cards.example: Improving scientific literacy helps the public resist misinformation.

cards.definition: Finding something that existed / creating something new.
cards.example: The invention of the printing press transformed education.
cards.warning: Se descubre lo que ya existía (penicillin); se inventa lo nuevo (the telephone).

cards.definition: To repeat a study and get the same results.
cards.example: Other scientists have been unable to replicate the results.

cards.definition: Progress in knowledge or technology.
cards.example: Medical advances have dramatically increased survival rates for many cancers.

title: Media & advertising
description: Prensa, publicidad, influencers y consumo de información.

cards.definition: Means of communication reaching large audiences.
cards.example: The mass media plays a powerful role in shaping public opinion.
collocations: the role of the mass media

cards.definition: To influence what people think.
cards.example: Newspapers can shape public opinion on immigration.

cards.definition: The reporting of an event by the media.
cards.example: Media coverage of climate change has increased substantially.

cards.definition: Unfairly favouring one side / fair and neutral.
cards.example: Public broadcasters are expected to provide impartial news.

cards.definition: Presenting news in a shocking way to attract attention.
cards.example: Tabloid newspapers are often criticised for sensationalism.

cards.definition: Popular newspaper / serious newspaper.
cards.example: Tabloids focus on celebrity gossip, while broadsheets cover politics in depth.

cards.definition: Online content designed to attract clicks rather than inform.
cards.example: Clickbait headlines often exaggerate or mislead.

cards.definition: The right of journalists to report without government control.
cards.example: Freedom of the press is a cornerstone of democracy.

cards.definition: Unjustified interference in someone's private life.
cards.example: Photographing celebrities' children is a clear invasion of privacy.

cards.definition: The group of people an advert or product is aimed at.
cards.example: Advertisers increasingly use social media to reach their target audience.

cards.definition: Able to convince / influencing people unfairly.
cards.example: Advertising aimed at children can be highly manipulative.

cards.definition: People who buy goods and services.
cards.example: Advertising creates desires that consumers did not know they had.

cards.definition: A company's product name / continuing to buy the same brand.
cards.example: Advertisers try to build brand loyalty from a young age.

cards.definition: A person who uses social media to influence followers, often to promote products.
cards.example: Many influencers fail to disclose that their posts are paid advertisements.

cards.definition: To publicly support a product, often for payment.
cards.example: Celebrity endorsements make products seem more desirable.

cards.definition: Giving a false idea.
cards.example: Misleading advertisements should be banned.

cards.definition: Valuing money and possessions too much.
cards.example: Constant advertising may make young people more materialistic.

cards.definition: Organisations that publish or broadcast news.
cards.example: Traditional news outlets are losing readers to online platforms.

cards.definition: News reported by ordinary people, often via social media.
cards.example: Citizen journalism can expose events that the mainstream media ignores.

cards.definition: To spread very quickly online.
cards.example: A single video can go viral and reach millions overnight.

cards.definition: To send out on TV or radio / a TV or radio company.
cards.example: Public broadcasters should be funded independently of the government.

cards.definition: Adverts shown based on a user's personal data.
cards.example: Targeted advertising relies on collecting huge amounts of personal data.

cards.definition: Advertisements on TV, radio or online.
cards.example: Several countries ban commercials during children's programmes.

cards.definition: The ability to critically evaluate media content.
cards.example: Schools should teach media literacy so pupils can identify fake news.

title: Tourism
description: Turismo de masas, ecoturismo, impacto económico y cultural de los viajes.

cards.definition: Tourism involving very large numbers of people.
cards.example: Mass tourism has transformed quiet fishing villages into crowded resorts.

cards.definition: Too many tourists in a place, harming residents and the environment.
cards.example: Venice and Barcelona have introduced measures to combat overtourism.

cards.definition: Tourism that protects nature and benefits local people.
cards.example: Ecotourism can provide an income while protecting rainforests.

cards.definition: A place that tourists visit.
cards.example: Spain is one of the world's most popular tourist destinations.

cards.definition: Income earned from tourism.
cards.example: Tourism revenue funds the restoration of historic monuments.

cards.definition: Jobs available only at certain times of year.
cards.example: Tourism often creates low-paid, seasonal employment.

cards.definition: A charge paid by visitors, often per night.
cards.example: A tourist tax could help cities cover the costs of cleaning and policing.

cards.definition: People who live in an area.
cards.example: Tourism should benefit local communities, not only international hotel chains.

cards.definition: Homes rented to visitors for a few days.
cards.example: The growth of short-term rentals has pushed up rents for locals.

cards.definition: Real and genuine, not artificial.
cards.example: Many travellers seek authentic experiences away from tourist traps.

cards.definition: An overpriced place designed to attract tourists.
cards.example: The main square is full of tourist traps selling expensive souvenirs.

cards.definition: Far from popular tourist places.
cards.example: I prefer travelling off the beaten track, where you meet more locals.

cards.definition: To widen one's experience and understanding.
cards.example: Travelling abroad broadens young people's horizons.

cards.definition: Sharing of ideas and customs between cultures.
cards.example: Tourism promotes cultural exchange and mutual understanding.

cards.definition: Changed to make money, losing original character.
cards.example: Some traditional festivals have become too commercialised.

cards.definition: A place where people go on holiday.
cards.example: Coastal resorts are crowded in summer and empty in winter.

cards.definition: Pressure on water, energy and services.
cards.example: Large numbers of tourists put a strain on water resources in dry regions.

cards.definition: How many people visit / limits on them.
cards.example: Machu Picchu introduced daily caps on visitor numbers.

cards.definition: Businesses such as hotels and restaurants.
cards.example: The hospitality industry employs millions of young people.

cards.definition: An object bought to remember a place.
cards.example: Locally made souvenirs support traditional crafts.

cards.definition: A place of historical importance / a famous building.
cards.example: Heritage sites suffer physical damage from millions of visitors.

cards.definition: Low-cost travel, usually with a rucksack, without a package tour.
cards.example: Backpacking through Asia taught me to be independent.

cards.definition: A holiday where travel and accommodation are sold together.
cards.example: Package holidays made foreign travel affordable for ordinary families.

cards.definition: Something essential for an economy to survive.
cards.example: For many islands, tourism is an economic lifeline.

title: Family & ageing
description: Estructuras familiares, crianza, relaciones intergeneracionales y vejez.

cards.definition: Parents and children / a family including grandparents, aunts, etc.
cards.example: In many cultures, the extended family is giving way to the nuclear family.

cards.definition: A family with only one parent.
cards.example: Single-parent families are more likely to experience financial hardship.

cards.definition: The way a child is raised.
cards.example: A child's upbringing has a lasting effect on their values.

cards.definition: The process of raising children / the approach used.
cards.example: Overprotective parenting may prevent children from becoming independent.

cards.definition: A person others look up to and copy.
cards.example: Parents are the most important role models for young children.

cards.definition: Differences in attitudes between young and old people.
cards.example: Technology has widened the generation gap in many families.

cards.definition: The number of births in a population.
cards.example: Falling birth rates mean there will be fewer workers to support pensioners.

cards.definition: Old people (polite terms).
cards.example: The elderly are particularly vulnerable to loneliness.
cards.warning: 'old people' puede sonar brusco; usa 'older people' o 'the elderly'.

cards.definition: Residential places where elderly people are cared for.
cards.example: In some cultures, sending parents to a care home is seen as abandoning them.

cards.definition: Money paid after retirement / the age people stop working.
cards.example: Many governments are raising the retirement age to keep pensions affordable.

cards.definition: People who rely on someone financially.
cards.example: Elderly people who are dependent on their children may feel like a burden.

cards.definition: A person who looks after someone ill, old or disabled.
cards.example: Unpaid family carers save the health service billions every year.

cards.definition: Looking after children while parents work.
cards.example: Affordable childcare allows more mothers to return to work.

cards.definition: Time off work for parents after a child is born.
cards.example: Equal parental leave encourages fathers to share childcare.

cards.definition: Routine tasks at home such as cleaning.
cards.example: Children who help with household chores learn responsibility.

cards.definition: With members who care about and support each other.
cards.example: I come from a close-knit family; we have lunch together every Sunday.

cards.definition: A close emotional connection.
cards.example: Shared meals strengthen the bond between parents and children.

cards.definition: Involving different generations.
cards.example: Intergenerational programmes bring students and retirees together.

cards.definition: Feeling alone / having little contact with others.
cards.example: Social isolation among older people is a growing public health issue.

cards.definition: Good judgement gained over time.
cards.example: Older employees bring valuable wisdom and life experience to the workplace.

cards.definition: Young adults who return to live with their parents.
cards.es: generación que vuelve a casa de los padres
cards.example: High rents have created a boomerang generation of graduates.

cards.definition: Long life.
cards.example: Japan is famous for the longevity of its population.

cards.definition: Brothers and sisters.
cards.example: Only children may miss out on the experience of growing up with siblings.

cards.definition: To give a child too much, harming their character / to treat with care.
cards.example: Grandparents often spoil their grandchildren.

title: Food & agriculture
description: Agricultura, seguridad alimentaria, desperdicio y hábitos alimentarios.

cards.definition: Reliable access to enough affordable, nutritious food.
cards.example: Climate change threatens food security in many developing countries.

cards.definition: Food thrown away instead of eaten.
cards.example: Supermarkets should donate unsold food to reduce food waste.

cards.definition: Producing large amounts of food using machines, chemicals and confined animals.
cards.example: Factory farming raises serious concerns about animal welfare.

cards.definition: Food grown without artificial chemicals.
cards.example: Organic produce is better for the soil but more expensive.
cards.note: 'produce' (sustantivo) = productos agrícolas; se acentúa en la 1.ª sílaba.

cards.definition: Chemicals that kill pests / chemicals that help plants grow.
cards.example: The overuse of pesticides has contributed to the decline of bees.

cards.definition: The amount of crops produced per area.
cards.example: New irrigation techniques have doubled crop yields.

cards.definition: Genetically modified plants.
cards.example: Supporters claim GM crops could end hunger; critics fear unknown risks.

cards.definition: Poor health from lack of food / an extreme shortage of food.
cards.example: Malnutrition still affects millions of children worldwide.

cards.definition: Produced nearby.
cards.example: Locally sourced food has a smaller carbon footprint.

cards.definition: The distance food travels from producer to consumer.
cards.example: Buying seasonal fruit reduces food miles.

cards.definition: A diet based mainly on plants rather than animal products.
cards.example: A shift to plant-based diets would cut agricultural emissions.

cards.definition: Farm animals such as cows, sheep and pigs.
cards.example: Livestock farming produces a large share of methane emissions.

cards.definition: The well-being and humane treatment of animals.
cards.example: Stricter laws on animal welfare would raise meat prices.

cards.definition: Supplying water to crops artificially.
cards.example: Agriculture accounts for around 70% of water use, mainly for irrigation.

cards.definition: A basic food eaten regularly.
cards.example: Rice is the staple food for over half the world's population.

cards.definition: Restaurant companies selling quick, cheap meals.
cards.example: The spread of fast-food chains has changed eating habits in Asia.

cards.definition: The way a person usually eats.
cards.example: Eating habits formed in childhood often last a lifetime.

cards.definition: Containing many nutrients / the amount of nutrients.
cards.example: School meals should be both affordable and nutritious.

cards.definition: Information on packaging about ingredients and nutrition.
cards.example: Clear food labelling helps consumers make healthier choices.

cards.definition: Farmers who work a small piece of land.
cards.example: Small-scale farmers cannot compete with large agribusinesses on price.

cards.definition: Large-scale, commercial agriculture.
cards.example: A few agribusiness giants control much of the global seed market.

cards.definition: The loss or damage of fertile soil.
cards.example: Overgrazing has caused severe soil erosion in the region.

cards.definition: Able to produce all one needs.
cards.example: Few countries are fully self-sufficient in food.

cards.definition: Food prepared at home.
cards.example: Busy families are eating fewer home-cooked meals than in the past.
